summary:
Wavelength is an interactive astronomical data exploration platform designed to help users explore how celestial objects and regions of the universe are observed over time.

The project integrates real astronomical observations from NASA's SPHEREx mission through the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA). Users can enter celestial coordinates (Right Ascension and Declination), retrieve available observations, explore their metadata, and visualize them through an interactive astronomical viewer. The platform also enables chronological image comparison and time-lapse exploration to make changes between observations easier to investigate.

By transforming complex astronomical datasets into an accessible and interactive scientific experience, Wavelength helps students, researchers, and astronomy enthusiasts explore infrared observations and investigate potential variable or moving sources.

The project is important because it bridges the gap between large-scale scientific archives and accessible astronomical research tools, encouraging data-driven discovery, scientific exploration, and broader public engagement with space science.
details:
Project Details — Wavelength

1. What Does the Project Do and How Does It Work?

Wavelength is an interactive astronomical data exploration platform designed to make real space observations more accessible and easier to investigate.

The platform connects users to NASA's SPHEREx astronomical data through the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA). Users can enter celestial coordinates (Right Ascension and Declination), select a Field of View, and search for available observations covering a specific region of the sky.

Retrieved observations can be explored through an astronomical viewer, with access to observation metadata, collection information, spectral bands, and original scientific data files. Wavelength is also designed around chronological exploration and visual comparison of available observations, helping users investigate how astronomical regions are observed across different observation times.

2. What Benefits Does It Provide?

Wavelength simplifies access to complex astronomical archives by bringing coordinate-based searching, observation retrieval, scientific visualization, and data exploration into one environment.

Its main benefits include:

  • Making authentic astronomical observations easier to access and explore.
  • Simplifying the discovery of observations covering specific celestial coordinates.
  • Providing observation metadata and traceable scientific data sources.
  • Supporting the exploration of infrared astronomical datasets.
  • Creating a more accessible experience for students, researchers, and astronomy enthusiasts.

3. What Is the Intended Impact?

Our goal is to bridge the gap between large scientific astronomical archives and accessible research tools.

Wavelength aims to encourage data-driven astronomical exploration, improve educational access to infrared astronomy, and help users investigate real observations without requiring them to navigate multiple complex scientific interfaces.

Ultimately, the project seeks to make scientific space data more understandable, interactive, and approachable for a wider community.

4. What Technologies and Tools Were Used?

The project combines web development with scientific Python technologies and official astronomical data services.

Platform and Backend:

  • Python — Scientific data processing.
  • FastAPI — Scientific processing service and API architecture.

Scientific Libraries:

  • Astropy — Astronomical data and FITS processing.
  • Astroquery — Access to astronomical archives.
  • PyVO — Virtual Observatory services and data retrieval.
  • NumPy and SciPy — Numerical and scientific computation.
  • Reproject — Astronomical image reprojection.
  • Astropy-HEALPix — HEALPix-based astronomical data handling.
  • Requests — External API communication.

Scientific Data Sources:

  • NASA/IPAC SPHEREx Archive.
  • SPHEREx SIA2 interface.
  • Gaia DR3 astronomical catalog services.

The project relies on real astronomical datasets rather than fabricated scientific observations.

5. How Is the Project Creative and Innovative?

Wavelength combines astronomical archive access, coordinate-based exploration, and scientific image visualization into a unified interactive experience.

Instead of treating astronomical observations as isolated files, the project focuses on connecting observations with their spatial coordinates, observation metadata, spectral information, and available observation times.

Its central creative idea is to transform complex astronomical data retrieval into an intuitive exploration workflow, making it easier for users to move from a celestial coordinate to actual scientific observations.

6. What Factors Did Our Team Consider?

Throughout development, we prioritized:

  • Scientific Accuracy: Using authentic astronomical data and documented scientific sources.
  • Data Traceability: Preserving observation identifiers, metadata, and original data references.
  • Image Integrity: Respecting original FITS structures, numerical pixel values, and available spatial resolution.
  • Accessibility: Making scientific exploration easier through an intuitive interface.
  • Performance: Supporting efficient data retrieval and progressive image visualization.
  • Reliability: Handling unavailable observations and external service errors transparently.
  • Scientific Responsibility: Distinguishing observed sources from unverified candidates and avoiding unsupported discovery claims.

Wavelength is an independent project developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 and does not represent an official NASA product or endorsement.
